# Data model

18 tables, grouped by the question they answer. The schema is deliberately ahead of the code: the
scheduler, alerting, and RBAC tables are complete and unused, because a column added later costs a
migration and an audit of every query, while a column carried unused costs nothing.

Drawn in four diagrams rather than one. All 18 tables in a single entity diagram is a picture nobody
reads.

## Identity and tenancy

Every tenant-scoped table carries `tenant_id` from the first migration. Retrofitting tenancy would mean a full-schema migration plus an audit of every query, so the column is carried unused rather than added later ([ADR-0008](../adr/0008-oidc-rbac-multitenancy.md)).

```mermaid
erDiagram
    tenants ||--o{ users : tenant_id
    tenants ||--o{ role_grants : tenant_id
    users ||--o{ role_grants : user_id
    roles ||--o{ role_grants : role_name
    users ||--o{ role_grants : granted_by
    tenants {
        uuid id PK
    }
    users {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
    }
    roles {
        text name PK
    }
    role_grants {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid user_id FK
        text role_name FK
        uuid environment_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
        uuid granted_by FK
    }
```

## Inventory

What is being watched, and how to reach it. Credentials are split: everything non-secret is on `connections`, while the password and any client private key go to the secrets provider under a name that row carries.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    environments ||--o{ instances : environment_id
    instances ||--o{ connections : instance_id
    environments {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
    }
    instances {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid environment_id FK
    }
    connections {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
    }
    secrets {
        uuid tenant_id FK
    }
```

## Operations

Scheduled work and its results. `jobs` carries the lease columns an at-most-once scheduler needs — `lease_owner`, `lease_expires_at`, `heartbeat_at` — which nothing writes yet.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    schedules ||--o{ jobs : schedule_id
    jobs ||--o{ backups : job_id
    schedules ||--o{ backups : schedule_id
    backups ||--o{ verifications : backup_id
    jobs ||--o{ verifications : job_id
    backups ||--o{ restores : backup_id
    jobs ||--o{ restores : job_id
    schedules {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
    }
    jobs {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid schedule_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
        uuid triggered_by FK
    }
    backups {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
        uuid job_id FK
        uuid schedule_id FK
        uuid triggered_by FK
    }
    verifications {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid backup_id FK
        uuid job_id FK
        uuid triggered_by FK
    }
    restores {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid backup_id FK
        uuid job_id FK
        uuid target_instance_id FK
        uuid triggered_by FK
    }
```

## Observability

Facts, conditions, and the record of who did what. `events` are facts; `alerts` are conditions with a lifecycle. `audit_log` has a trigger that rejects UPDATE and DELETE, because an audit log that can be edited is not evidence.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    alert_rules ||--o{ alerts : rule_id
    alert_rules {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid environment_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
    }
    alerts {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid rule_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
        uuid acknowledged_by FK
    }
    notifiers {
        uuid id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
    }
    events {
        bigint id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid instance_id FK
    }
    audit_log {
        bigint id PK
        uuid tenant_id FK
        uuid user_id FK
    }
```
